result:
The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old, standing on a pebbled beach in Maine with my father. The wind was sharp, carrying the scent of salt and seaweed, and the waves crashed against the shore with a rhythm that felt like a heartbeat. My father knelt beside me, his hands rough from years of work, and pointed to the horizon. "See that?" he said. "That’s where the world ends and everything else begins."

I didn’t understand then, but I do now. The ocean is a paradox—endless yet finite, powerful yet fragile. It gives life and takes it. It’s a mirror, reflecting the sky’s moods, and a veil, hiding depths we’ll never fully explore. I’ve stood on its shores countless times since, each visit a reminder of how small I am in the grand scheme of things.

Sometimes, when the world feels too loud, I close my eyes and imagine the sound of the waves. It’s a kind of white noise, a constant that doesn’t judge or demand. The ocean doesn’t care about my mistakes or my worries. It just *is*.

I wonder if that’s why we’re drawn to it—the way it humbles us, makes us feel both insignificant and part of something vast. Maybe we need the ocean to remind us that life isn’t just about us. It’s about the tides, the currents, the unseen creatures in the deep, the way the moon pulls the water toward it.

The ocean teaches patience. It doesn’t rush. It doesn’t panic. It simply *moves*. And in that movement, there’s a kind of peace.
